example: Speak directly to a named person or the reader: “Reader, you would have trusted him too.”
Introduce something with “There is” or “There was”: “There was a second heartbeat inside the room.”
Highlight one detail with “It was … that …”: “It was the missing button that betrayed him.”
Make an -ing action the subject of the sentence: “Keeping secrets had become her profession.”
Open with two possibilities joined by “Either … or …”: “Either the map was wrong or the island had moved.”
Link two changing conditions with “The … the …”: “The closer she came, the quieter the house grew.”
Lead with an extreme quality and its consequence: “So thin was the ice that we could see the coins beneath it.”
Open with a comparison using “Like” or “As”: “Like a loose tooth, the tower shifted in the wind.”
Begin by defining what something means to a character: “Home meant whichever room she could lock.”
Begin with a collection of telling details: “A bent nail, two receipts, and a tooth lay on the desk.”
Lead with an exact distance, quantity, or dimension: “Six inches separated the blade from his throat.”
Name the source of a claim before giving it: “According to the ledger, she had died twice.”
Begin with an unverified claim circulating among people: “Word was the ferryman accepted memories as payment.”
Open with a character recalling something: “I remembered the gate being taller.”
Point ahead to a future realization or consequence: “Later, she would understand why he wore gloves.”
Begin by acknowledging something difficult or revealing: “I confess that I wanted the letter to be a threat.”
Lead with an assurance or commitment: “You have my word: the door will stay open.”
Open with a broad observation about how the world works: “Small towns keep excellent records of other people’s mistakes.”
Revise the opening claim as the sentence unfolds: “Seven men—six, counting only the living—returned.”
Repeat a word from the preceding sentence’s ending at the start of the next. After a sentence ending in “mercy”: “Mercy had never entered his calculations.”
Begin by giving something nonhuman a human motive or action: “The house resented every visitor.”
Open with an apparent contradiction that carries a deeper truth: “His freedom depended on staying locked inside.”
Introduce something serious in deliberately mild terms: “The missing roof presented a minor inconvenience.”
Draw attention to an absence before explaining it: “One name was missing from the passenger list.”
